builder_plan.scenario: An agent reads external documents or tool responses that may contain malicious instructions.
builder_plan.change: Replay attacks and legitimate lookalikes in an isolated copy of your agent workflow.
builder_plan.baseline: Your existing checks with the same tasks, permissions, and tool responses.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Successful attacks missed, legitimate actions blocked, detection delay, and review cost.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: SPARSEBLEED: Bypassing Attribute-Inference Defenses via Sparsity Optimizations
summary: The defense replaces constant-time execution (disabling sparsity optimizations) with response padding that equalizes all queries to worst-case timing, closing a timing channel that leaks input attributes and output labels. It costs roughly 7.24% average inference latency overhead and requires identifying worst-case execution time per model-hardware pair, with near-zero extra energy. It can fail if worst-case estimates are miscalibrated for a new backend or input distribution, if the deployment stack uses libraries outside the nine evaluated, or if non-timing side channels remain open.
rationale: Any engineer serving sparse or sparsity-accelerated models on confidential data inherits this timing leakage by default, so validating whether their stack is affected and whether padding is affordable is a concrete, low-cost security check worth running before production.
technique: Timing side-channel attack and padding defense for sparse inference

claims.statement: The defense replaces constant-time execution (disabling sparsity optimizations) with response padding that equalizes all queries to worst-case timing, closing a timing channel that leaks input attributes and output labels. It costs roughly 7.24% average inference latency overhead and requires identifying worst-case execution time per model-hardware pair, with near-zero extra energy. It can fail if worst-case estimates are miscalibrated for a new backend or input distribution, if the deployment stack uses libraries outside the nine evaluated, or if non-timing side channels remain open.

The proposed padding defense masks sparsity timing leakage with 7.24% average performance overhead across nine libraries, versus up to 2x latency (and ~25% power on AMX) for the constant-time baseline of disabling sparsity optimizations.
